package_info.package_name: N/A (RepoJacking attack enables arbitrary malicious package creation)
package_info.package_manager: Go/Swift/PHP (any language that pulls code directly from GitHub repositories)
package_info.package_versions: All versions of packages whose GitHub repositories were hijacked via RepoJacking
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is considered malicious because attackers can take over the original repository namespace and publish code under a trusted name, serving arbitrary malicious code to users and applications that depend on the original repository. This enables attackers to inject and distribute any code, including credential stealers and remote payload droppers, under the guise of a legitimate package.

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when package is fetched from hijacked repository)
execution_context.file_location: main.go (or equivalent entrypoint in the hijacked repository)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code accesses the SECRET_TOKEN environment variable, sends its value to a hardcoded external domain via HTTP POST, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code programmatically reads a sensitive environment variable (SECRET_TOKEN) and transmits it to an external server controlled by the attacker, which is a direct credential exfiltration technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate open-source packages do not access unrelated environment variables or transmit secrets to external domains during import or build processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some packages may send telemetry or error reports, but these should never include sensitive environment variables or secrets, and should only communicate with trusted, documented endpoints.
key_indicators: Access to environment variables unrelated to package function
Hardcoded external domain for exfiltration (e.g., https://attacker.com/exfil)
Network requests initiated during import or build phase
Use of HTTP POST to transmit potentially sensitive data

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when package is fetched from hijacked repository)
execution_context.file_location: main.swift (or equivalent entrypoint in the hijacked repository)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code downloads a remote payload from a hardcoded external domain and writes it to the local filesystem, enabling further compromise of the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code automatically downloads a file from an attacker-controlled URL and writes it to disk without user knowledge or consent, which is a common initial stage of malware delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not fetch and write remote code or binaries to the filesystem during import or build, especially from untrusted or undocumented sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Auto-updaters or dependency managers may fetch files, but only with explicit user consent and from trusted, well-documented sources. They do not silently download and write arbitrary payloads.
key_indicators: Hardcoded external URL for payload download (e.g., https://attacker.com/payload)
Automatic download and write to filesystem during import/build
No user interaction or consent required
Writes to system locations such as /tmp/payload

attack_chain.action: Attacker claims a previously retired GitHub namespace by creating a repository with the target name and then renaming their account to match the original owner.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains control over the trusted repository namespace, making it possible to impersonate the original package.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads malicious code to the hijacked repository, replacing or augmenting the original codebase.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is now served to all users and systems fetching the package from the hijacked repository.

attack_chain.action: Users or CI systems import or build the package, causing the malicious code to execute automatically.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential exfiltration, remote payload delivery, and potential further compromise of user systems or CI environments.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected network requests initiated during package import or build processes
Access to environment variables or sensitive files in package code unrelated to documented functionality
Automatic download and writing of remote payloads to the filesystem without user interaction
file_indicators: Sudden changes or additions in main.go, main.swift, or other entrypoint files in a previously trusted repository
Presence of hardcoded external URLs (e.g., https://attacker.com/exfil, https://attacker.com/payload) in source code
References to exfiltration or payload delivery endpoints within code
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains not previously associated with the package, such as attacker.com
Connections to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., attacker.com/exfil, attacker.com/payload) during import or build
Unusual network activity from build or CI environments to unknown external endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor for changes in trusted repositories, especially following account renames or repository transfers. Flag packages that initiate network requests or access sensitive environment variables during import or build. Alert on the presence of hardcoded external domains or URLs in package code. Track and investigate unexpected outbound connections from build or CI environments to unknown or untrusted domains, and correlate with recent package updates or repository ownership changes.
